query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tribo‐corrosion in HEAs is governed by the dynamic disruption of the native passivating surface film by mechanical wear, which exposes underlying, compositionally heterogeneous phases. This leads to the formation of local micro‐galvanic cells that accelerate corrosion rates beyond the sum of separate wear and corrosion effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy fabricated in a stable, well-annealed condition that naturally forms a protective oxide film enriched in more noble elements.
generation.intervention: Apply a sliding wear load on the HEA in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) to actively erode the protective film while allowing corrosion to occur.
generation.conditions: Conduct tests at room temperature comparing (a) samples under static immersion (corrosion only) and (b) samples under controlled sliding wear in the same corrosive environment, ensuring that mechanical loading is sufficient to disrupt the passive film.
generation.structural_mediator: Disruption and removal of the robust passive oxide layer, exposing regions with distinct phase chemistries (e.g., less noble areas) that can act as anodic sites for localized galvanic corrosion.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding wear, the protective layer is mechanically removed, which exposes the underlying heterogeneous microstructure. This differential exposure creates micro-galvanic couples between nobler and less noble phases. The resulting electrochemical cells intensify localized corrosion, while the absence of a continuous film further increases the wear rate, leading to a coupled degradation effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline (static corrosion or wear in inert environments), the combined tribo-corrosion condition will exhibit an overall higher degradation rate. Specifically, one should observe increased wear track volumes (due to the loss of film protection) and higher localized corrosion attacks (evidenced by accelerated weight loss or electrochemical activity) because of the synergistic galvanic effect.
generation.baseline: Parallel tests performed in a non-corrosive environment to isolate wear effects and static corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl to isolate corrosion effects.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold when the native film is modestly robust and can be consistently disrupted by wear. It may fail in cases where the alloy’s film self-heals very rapidly or if the applied wear energy is too low to remove the film effectively.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative increase in corrosion rate due to wear-induced film disruption and subsequent galvanic coupling is uncertain and likely depends on the specific alloy composition and microstructural details. Further experimental calibration is needed to determine precise values.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA samples and subject one set to static immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl (to evaluate corrosion alone) and another set to combined sliding wear in the same solution under identical environmental conditions. Monitor surface films in real time using in situ techniques (such as scanning Kelvin probe microscopy) and post-test characterization (using SEM/EDS) to assess film continuity and localized corrosion pits. Additionally, measure weight loss and track wear volumes.
measurements: Total weight loss and mass loss vs. time
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization, EIS) to assess corrosion rate
Wear track analysis (depth, volume) via profilometry or microscopy
Surface compositional mapping and film integrity assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tribo-corrosion tests do not show a statistically significant synergistic increase in both wear damage and corrosion rates beyond the additive effects observed for isolated wear and static corrosion – or if surface analysis does not reveal evidence of disrupted film and localized galvanic cells – then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
